versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 37 This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his officials. 38 So Pharaoh asked them, “Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?”

39 Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has made all this known to you, there is no one as discerning and wise as you. 40 You shall be in charge of my house, and all my people are to obey your commands. Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you.”

41 Pharaoh also told Joseph, “I hereby place you over all the land of Egypt.” 42 Then Pharaoh removed the signet ring from his finger, put it on Joseph’s finger, clothed him in garments of fine linen, and placed a gold chain around his neck. 43 He had Joseph ride in his second chariot, with men calling out before him, “Bow the knee!” So he placed him over all the land of Egypt.
44 And Pharaoh declared to Joseph, “I am Pharaoh, but without your permission, no one in all the land of Egypt shall lift his hand or foot.”
45 Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and he gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife. And Joseph took charge of all the land of Egypt.

context_lines: Pharaoh and his officials approve Joseph's proposal. Pharaoh recognizes that God has made the matter known to Joseph and that his wisdom fits the responsibility he has described. He places Joseph over his household and all Egypt, reserving only the throne for himself.

The appointment is made public through concrete signs: Pharaoh's signet ring, fine linen, a gold chain, and a ride in the second chariot. People are called to bow before Joseph. These actions give public force to the king's declaration that Joseph's authority must be respected throughout the land.

Pharaoh also gives him an Egyptian name, Zaphenath-paneah, and Asenath, daughter of Potiphera the priest of On, as his wife. The man who entered Egypt as a slave is now entrusted with the nation's preparations for famine. His new place in Egyptian society will also become the setting for the birth of his sons.

The reversal is striking beside the earlier chapters. His brothers stripped him of a robe, and a later garment was used to accuse him falsely. Now he receives clothing and other signs of honor from the king. The authority shown in his youthful dreams is beginning to take a public form, though his family does not yet know what has happened.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand the appointment as Joseph's vindication and preparation to preserve life in the famine. [Wesley's note on Genesis 41:44](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) also draws a Christian comparison with the authority given to Christ. The comparison follows the movement from suffering to honor and from personal authority to care for others.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 7:9–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/7.htm) directly identifies Joseph's appointment as the result of God giving him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh. The man his brothers sold is the one God places in a position that will help them survive. Their rejection has not defeated God's purpose for the family.

Joseph's rise also offers an established parallel to the honor and authority given to Jesus, as [Wesley's Genesis 41:44 note](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) recognizes. [Philippians 2:8–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/philippians/2.htm) joins Jesus' obedient suffering with God's exalting Him and every knee bowing. Joseph's delegated rule over Egypt helps illustrate the pattern, while Jesus' lordship extends far beyond one nation and one crisis.
